Searching Lanka; Mandodari Mistaken for Sita

Stories from the Ramayana

Searching Lanka; Mandodari Mistaken for Sita

The Pushpaka Vimana, Sleeping Queens, and a Wrong Recognition

Everyday telling — Sundara Kanda, sargas 4–14

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read it slowly, as if you were sitting at home among everyone, telling it to them.

This book is a story of a search. Lanka at night, house after house, the Pushpaka Vimana, sleeping queens — where Lanka shines, bring wonder into your voice; where Mandodari appears, lower your voice; where Hanuman despairs, make your voice heavy; where the Ashoka grove appears, bring new hope into your voice.

There are no yellow boxes in this book. Hanuman speaks in his own mind — his thoughts come inside the story itself. Change your voice a little as you speak them — firm in the search, startled in the mistake, heavy in despair, firm in resolve.

(The purple cues) tell you when to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak.

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sargas 4–14 — the search of Lanka and the mistaking of Mandodari. The meeting with Lankini is in the book before this one. Anything else you may want to know about the story is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Hanuman — Sugriva's minister, son of Vayu the wind. A powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, a long tail, a gentle and devoted face, a saffron dhoti. At night, in a tiny form, he is searching Lanka for Sita.

Ravana — king of Lanka, lord of the rakshasas. Tall, majestic, dark as a black cloud, long arms, red eyes, a tall golden crown, a single head. In this book he is seen asleep.

Mandodari — Ravana's chief queen. Beautiful, adorned, asleep in calm — whom Hanuman for a few moments takes to be Sita.

Vibhishana — Ravana's younger brother. Held to be dharmic — his house is white and peaceful. He does not appear in person in this book, but his house catches Hanuman's eye.

Kumbhakarna — Ravana's brother, a great warrior. Hanuman sees his vast house too.

Prahasta — Ravana's commander. His house also comes in the search.

Sita — Rama's wife. She does not appear in person in this book — but the whole search is for her.

1 · The Search Begins in Lanka · · THE SEARCH BEGINS IN LANKA

Hanuman was inside Lanka — in his tiny form, in the darkness of the night. Lankini had blessed him — “Roam, and search for Sita.”

And Hanuman began his search — house by house, mansion by mansion. He went from one house to another — climbing onto roofs, peering through windows, looking into courtyards.

What houses Lanka had! Golden doors, platforms of gems, tall mansions, beautiful gardens — and lamps burning in every house.

Hanuman looked into every house — “Is Sita here?” But in every house were the families of the rakshasas — asleep, eating, talking — and Sita was nowhere.

He went on — and on. The night grew deeper — and the search grew longer.

Pause and think — Hanuman is searching house by house — on rooftops, through windows. Is patience the greatest strength in a search? And when something is very big — like the whole of Lanka — should it be searched in small parts?

2 · The Chiefs' Houses · · THE CHIEFS' HOUSES

Hanuman went into the houses of the rakshasa chiefs — the house of Prahasta, and the houses of the other chiefs. They were great mansions — of gold, of gems — and in them the rakshasas slept.

Then he went to Kumbhakarna's house — vast, splendid — and Sita was not there either.

Then he stopped before another house — and something felt different. That house was white — peaceful — and there was no noise in it.

This was Vibhishana's house — the house of Ravana's younger brother. Hanuman thought — (slowly, in a thoughtful voice) “This house is not like the others. There is peace here — some dharmic man must live here.”

He looked into that house too — but Sita was not there either.

Hanuman went on — toward Ravana's palace.

Pause and think — Vibhishana's house was white and peaceful — and Hanuman felt that some dharmic man lived there. Does a house also tell who lives in it? And when all houses look alike, should one pay attention to the house that is different?

3 · Ravana's Palace · · RAVANA'S PALACE

Hanuman came to Ravana's palace — and that palace was the greatest of all. High walls, golden doors, stairways of gems — and inside, the light of lamps.

In the courtyards of the palace were gardens — of flowers, of creepers — and the nests of birds. From inside the palace came the sound of music — and fragrance spread everywhere.

Hanuman thought — “If Sita is in Lanka, she will be here — in Ravana's palace.”

He began to enter the palace — slowly, in his tiny form, in the light of the lamps.

Pause and think — Ravana's palace was the greatest of all — and Hanuman thought Sita would be there. Is the greatest thing always found in the greatest place — or is it sometimes in a small place?

4 · The Pushpaka Vimana · · THE PUSHPAKA VIMANA

As soon as he entered the palace, Hanuman's eyes were dazzled — for before him stood the Pushpaka Vimana.

What a vimana the Pushpaka was! Vishwakarma had built it for Kubera — and Ravana had taken it from Kubera. It was of gold, studded with gems, and many-storied — like a palace that could fly in the sky.

What rooms the vimana had! In one room were paintings — in another, ivory — in a third, crystal. There were walls of gold — and windows of gems.

Hanuman thought — (in a wondering voice) “This is not a palace — this is a flying city!”

He went inside the vimana — room by room, storey by storey — and kept looking everywhere — “Is Sita here?”

Pause and think — Vishwakarma built the Pushpaka Vimana for Kubera — and Ravana took it. Is taking someone else's beautiful thing also a wrong? And Hanuman searched inside the vimana too — should any place be left out of a search?

5 · Inside the Pushpaka · · INSIDE THE PUSHPAKA

Hanuman wandered inside the vimana — and every room filled him with wonder.

In one room were golden statues — in another, lamps of gems — in a third, beautiful paintings — in which gods, gandharvas and apsaras were drawn.

In one room was a place to sit — golden seats, thrones of gems — and in one room was a place to sleep — great beds, sheets of silk.

Hanuman looked in every room — stopped by every bed — looked at every painting — but Sita was nowhere.

He came out of the vimana — and moved deeper into the palace.

Pause and think — Inside the Pushpaka Vimana every room was beautiful — but Sita was nowhere. Is what we search for always found in a beautiful place — or is beauty sometimes empty?

6 · Ravana Asleep · · RAVANA ASLEEP

Inside the palace Hanuman saw a great room — and in it a great bed. On the bed someone was asleep — and Hanuman stopped.

It was Ravana — king of the rakshasas. He was dark as a black cloud — his arms were long — his eyes were red — and his tall golden crown had slipped a little to one side.

On his body was a paste of red sandal — and garlands around his neck. He wore a white silk upper cloth — which had slipped down — and a yellow silk lower cloth. He breathed like a serpent — deep, heavy.

Hanuman looked at him — and stepped back. He thought — “This is Ravana — the one everyone speaks of. But where is Sita?”

He went on — toward the queens' chamber.

Pause and think — Hanuman saw Ravana asleep — and stepped back. Does even a sleeping enemy still frighten? And Ravana was asleep — but where was Sita?

7 · Mandodari — Is This Sita? · · MANDODARI — IS THIS SITA?

In the queens' chamber Hanuman saw a bed — of gold and ivory, studded with diamonds — and on it a woman was asleep.

That woman was beautiful — adorned — and asleep in calm. Around her the other queens slept — and the room shone with lamps.

Hanuman looked at her — and a wave of joy ran through his heart. He thought — (slowly, in a joyful voice) “This is Sita! This is Rama's wife! I have found her!”

He rejoiced — and his heart filled with gladness. So long a search — and now Sita was found!

But then a question rose in his mind — “Is this really Sita?”

Pause and think — Hanuman looked at Mandodari — and thought she was Sita. Does joy sometimes make us see what we wish to see? And when something is found too quickly, should it be checked and looked at again?

8 · The Mistake Breaks · · THE MISTAKE BREAKS

Hanuman looked again — carefully, slowly — and he understood — this was not Sita.

This woman was adorned — dressed in jewels, in silk garments, asleep in calm — beside Ravana. Sita could not be like this. Sita would be in grief — not adorned, not calm, not beside Ravana.

And the description Rama had given of Sita — it did not match this woman. Rama had said — Sita is simple, grieving, and lives in the memory of her husband.

Hanuman felt shame at his own mistake. He thought — “How could I think this was Sita? I came to search — and I fell into confusion.”

He saluted that woman — in his mind — and went on. She was Mandodari — Ravana's chief queen — and Hanuman knew her now.

Pause and think — Hanuman recognised his own mistake — and felt shame. Is recognising one's own mistake also a strength? And Rama had described Sita — does a description also help in a search?

9 · The Banquet Hall · · THE BANQUET HALL

Hanuman went on — and came into a great room — the banquet hall. The night's feast had been held there — and now everything lay scattered.

In the plates was leftover food — in the vessels, leftover drink — and garlands of flowers lay scattered.

In the room women slept — with their musical instruments. One had a veena — one a mridangam — one a flute. They had played music in the first part of the night and grown tired — and now they slept.

Hanuman looked in the banquet hall too — in every corner, beside every plate — but Sita was not there either.

He came out of the banquet hall — and climbed onto the roof of the palace.

Pause and think — In the banquet hall food lay scattered — and women slept with their instruments. Do feasts and music also grow tired? And Hanuman searched the banquet hall too — should any room be left out of a search?

10 · Hanuman's Grief · · HANUMAN'S GRIEF

Hanuman sat down on the roof of the palace — and grief filled his heart.

He thought — “I have searched every house of Lanka — every palace, every room, the Pushpaka Vimana, the queens' chamber, the banquet hall — and Sita has been found nowhere.”

“Is Sita dead? Has Ravana killed her? Is she hidden somewhere — where I cannot reach?”

Hanuman reproached himself — “I came to search for Sita — and I will return empty-handed? What will Sugriva say? What will Rama say? What will Angada and all the vanaras say?”

Despair filled his heart — and he sat on the roof — in the darkness of the night, alone.

Pause and think — Hanuman searched everywhere — and Sita was not found. Is failing in a search also a grief? And when someone says “I have done everything”, has everything truly been done — or is some place left?

11 · Not Defeat — the Ashoka Grove · · NOT DEFEAT — THE ASHOKA GROVE

Hanuman sat on the roof — despairing, grieving — and then he looked into the distance.

Behind the palace, far away, a garden could be seen — green and lush, full of flowers — and in its midst a great Ashoka tree.

It was the Ashoka grove — Ravana's garden. Hanuman thought — (slowly, in a voice of new hope) “I searched every house — but I did not search the garden! I did not look in the Ashoka grove!”

New hope woke in his heart — “If Sita is anywhere, she may be in the grove — where there are flowers, where there is peace.”

Hanuman stood up — and came down from the roof, and set out toward the grove.

Pause and think — Hanuman was in despair — and then he saw the Ashoka grove. Can a new place also be seen in despair? And when every place has been searched, should one more place be searched?

12 · Entering the Ashoka Grove · · ENTERING THE ASHOKA GROVE

Hanuman entered the Ashoka grove — and its beauty filled him with wonder.

In the grove were trees — Ashoka, champaka, mango, and flowering trees. The fragrance of flowers spread everywhere — and birds sang.

In the midst of the grove stood a great Ashoka tree — tall, green and lush, laden with flowers. Hanuman looked at that tree — and hope woke in his heart.

He went on into the grove — slowly, in his tiny form, between the trees — and kept looking everywhere — “Is Sita here?”

And here this story pauses — at the gate of the Ashoka grove, before a great Ashoka tree, and with a question — Is Sita here?

Pause and think — Hanuman entered the Ashoka grove — and hope woke in his heart. Is entering a new place also a new hope? And when someone says “no place is left”, is a grove also a place?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this book Hanuman searched Lanka house by house — the chiefs' houses, Ravana's palace, the Pushpaka Vimana, the queens' chamber, the banquet hall — and Sita was found nowhere. He took Mandodari for Sita — and then recognised his own mistake.

Then he fell into despair — and sat on the roof of the palace. But then he saw the Ashoka grove — and entered it with new hope.

Ask the listeners:

1. Hanuman is searching house by house — is patience the greatest strength in a search?

2. Vibhishana's house was white and peaceful — does a house also tell who lives in it?

3. The Pushpaka Vimana was beautiful — but Sita was not there. Is what we search for always found in a beautiful place?

4. Hanuman took Mandodari for Sita — does joy sometimes make us see what we wish to see?

5. Hanuman recognised his own mistake — is recognising one's own mistake also a strength?

6. Hanuman fell into despair — is failing in a search also a grief?

7. Hanuman saw the Ashoka grove — can a new place also be seen in despair?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sargas 4–14 — the search of Lanka and the mistaking of Mandodari.

The search begins in Lanka — sarga 4

Hanuman searching Lanka house by house at night, in his tiny form; the golden doors, the jewelled platforms, the houses lit with lamps — this is in sarga 4.

The chiefs' houses — sarga 5

The houses of Prahasta and the other chiefs; Kumbhakarna's vast house; Vibhishana's white and peaceful house, where Hanuman senses a dharmic man living — this is in sarga 5.

Ravana's palace — sarga 6

The compound of Ravana's palace — high walls, golden doors, gardens, music and fragrance — this is in sarga 6.

The Pushpaka Vimana — sargas 7–8

The sight of the Pushpaka Vimana — built by Vishwakarma for Kubera, taken by Ravana; many-storied, studded with gold and gems; rooms with paintings, ivory, crystal — described across two sargas, sargas 7–8.

Ravana asleep — sarga 9

Hanuman entering the palace and seeing Ravana asleep — dark as a black cloud, red eyes, long arms, crown askew, red sandal paste, white silk upper cloth, yellow silk lower cloth, breathing like a serpent — this is in sarga 9.

Mandodari — is this Sita? — sarga 10

Hanuman seeing Mandodari among the sleeping queens and taking her for Sita; his joy — this is in sarga 10.

The mistake breaks — sarga 10

Hanuman looking again and recognising his mistake — an adorned woman asleep in calm beside Ravana cannot be Sita; Rama's description of Sita does not match; shame at his own mistake — this is in sarga 10.

The banquet hall — sarga 11

The banquet hall — leftover food and drink, scattered garlands, women asleep with their musical instruments — this is in sarga 11.

Hanuman's grief — sarga 12

Hanuman's grief — he searched everywhere and Sita was found nowhere; is Sita dead, has Ravana killed her; reproaching himself — this is in sarga 12.

Not defeat — the Ashoka grove — sarga 13

Hanuman in despair on the palace roof seeing the Ashoka grove in the distance and resolving to search it — this is in sarga 13.

Entering the Ashoka grove — sarga 14

Hanuman entering the Ashoka grove — trees, flowers, birds, and the great Ashoka tree — this is in sarga 14.

What happens next

Hanuman has entered the Ashoka grove — and here this book pauses. The finding of Sita is in sarga 15 — her story is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of the search of Lanka pauses — at the gate of the Ashoka grove, before a great Ashoka tree, and with a question — is Sita here?

And whenever it feels to you that you have searched everywhere and found nothing, remember Hanuman — who saw the Ashoka grove from the roof of the palace, and entered it with new hope.

— The End —
